plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single pressure-temperature plot headed H2O. The vertical axis reads "Pressure, p (atm)" with ticks at 0.006, 1, and 218, and the horizontal axis reads "Temperature, T (C)" with ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374, the spacing on both visibly nonlinear. Two red curves meet at a filled dot labeled "Triple point" at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degrees, with dashed guide lines running to both axes. From that dot one branch rises almost vertically and leans slightly left, while the other sweeps up and to the right, ending at a second filled dot labeled "Critical point" at 218 atm and 374 degrees; below the triple point a single curve continues toward the lower left. Italic letters mark the regions the curves carve out: s at the left, l in the wedge between the branches, and v at the right. Curved arrows tag the branches "Melting", "Boiling", and "Sublimation", and a dashed pair marks the crossing at 1 atm and 100 degrees. Locating a point against these curves tells the reader which phase water occupies there. The plot lays out the coexistence boundaries, including the leftward-leaning melting line whose negative slope means added pressure can melt ice.

interactionPlan.concept: A substance's phase is fixed entirely by where its (T, p) state point lies relative to the coexistence curves; the leftward-leaning melting line means pressure alone can melt ice, and which transitions a heating path crosses depends on the pressure at which it is run.

interactions.label: Temperature T (°C)
interactions.teaches: Moving the state point horizontally changes phase only when it crosses a coexistence curve — phase is read off location, not off temperature alone

interactions.label: Pressure p (atm)
interactions.teaches: Raising pressure at a fixed sub-zero temperature pushes the state point across the left-leaning melting line, flipping the phase from solid to liquid — added pressure melts ice

interactions.label: Heating path (constant p)
interactions.teaches: The same heating (rising T) produces melting then boiling at 1 atm, sublimation at low pressure, and no sharp transition above the critical pressure — the path's pressure decides which boundaries are crossed

demo_steps.title: Phase = location
demo_steps.narration: Drag the temperature and pressure sliders: the state point moves and the solid, liquid, or vapor region tints beneath it. Wherever the point sits relative to the three red curves determines the phase.

demo_steps.title: Pressure melts ice
demo_steps.narration: Hold temperature just below 0 °C and raise the pressure slider. The point crosses the leftward-leaning melting curve and the highlighted region flips from solid to liquid — because that boundary has a negative slope, squeezing ice turns it to water.

demo_steps.title: Normal heating at 1 atm
demo_steps.narration: At 1 atm the horizontal path crosses the melting line near 0 °C (solid to liquid) and the boiling line at 100 °C (liquid to vapor) — the everyday sequence of melting then boiling.

demo_steps.title: Low-pressure heating: sublimation
demo_steps.narration: Drop the path below the triple-point pressure (0.006 atm). The horizontal line now crosses only the sublimation curve, so solid turns directly to vapor with no liquid stage.

demo_steps.title: Supercritical heating
demo_steps.narration: Raise the path above 218 atm, past the critical point. The line crosses no coexistence curve at all: liquid and vapor merge into one supercritical fluid, so there is no sharp boiling transition.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Phase is not a property of temperature or pressure alone but of the (T, p) point's position relative to the coexistence curves — which is why a negatively sloped melting line lets pressure melt ice, and why the same heating produces boiling, sublimation, or nothing depending on the pressure of the path.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Render as an SVG diagram with nonlinear (visually log-like) axes: y ticks 0.006, 1, 218 spaced so 1 sits low and 218 near the top; x ticks 0, 0.01, 100, 374 with 0.01 hugging 0 and 100/374 spread right. Draw the three coexistence curves in a single red stroke meeting at a black filled 'Triple point' dot (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm) and the boiling branch terminating at a black filled 'Critical point' dot (374 °C, 218 atm); the melting branch must visibly lean LEFT of vertical. Add gray dashed guide lines from both dots to the axes and a dashed pair at (100 °C, 1 atm). Place italic serif 's', 'l', 'v' in the left, central-wedge, and right regions. Tag the curves with small curved arrows labeled Melting, Boiling, Sublimation. Overlay a draggable-looking state dot driven by the two sliders, tint the containing region with a soft translucent fill (e.g. blue-ish for l, gray for s, orange for v), and draw the constant-pressure heating path as a horizontal line with small markers + labels at each curve crossing. Keep axis labels and the H2O title in the original bold styling.

authoredContext:
The figure shows the phase diagram for water. Using the graph, if you know the pressure and temperature, you can determine the phase of water. The solid curves—boundaries between phases—indicate phase transitions, that is, temperatures and pressures at which the phases coexist. For example, the boiling point of water is 100°C at 1.00 atm. As the pressure increases, the boiling temperature rises gradually to 374°C at a pressure of 218 atm. A pressure cooker (or even a covered pot) cooks food faster than an open pot, because the water can exist as a liquid at temperatures greater than 100°C without all boiling away. (As we’ll see in the next section, liquid water conducts heat better than steam or hot air.) The boiling point curve ends at a certain point called the critical point—that is, a critical temperature, above which the liquid and gas phases cannot be distinguished; the substance is called a supercritical fluid. At sufficiently high pressure above the critical point, the gas has the density of a liquid but does not condense. Carbon dioxide, for example, is supercritical at all temperatures above 31.0°C. Critical pressure is the pressure of the critical point.

Similarly, the curve between the solid and liquid regions in the figure gives the melting temperature at various pressures. For example, the melting point is 0°C at 1.00 atm, as expected. Water has the unusual property that ice is less dense than liquid water at the melting point, so at a fixed temperature, you can change the phase from solid (ice) to liquid (water) by increasing the pressure. That is, the melting temperature of ice falls with increased pressure, as the phase diagram shows. For example, when a car is driven over snow, the increased pressure from the tires melts the snowflakes; afterwards, the water refreezes and forms an ice layer.

The phase diagram (pT graph) for water shows solid (s), liquid (l), and vapor (v) phases. At temperatures and pressure above those of the critical point, there is no distinction between liquid and vapor. Note that the axes are nonlinear and the graph is not to scale. This graph is simplified—it omits several exotic phases of ice at higher pressures. The phase diagram of water is unusual because the melting-point curve has a negative slope, showing that you can melt ice by increasing the pressure.

Graph of pressure P in atmosphere versus temperature T in degree Celsius for water. The curve starts with going up and right to a point labeled triple point. This is at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degree C. From here, the curve diverges into two branches. One goes up and left and is almost vertical. The other goes up and right. On the branch going up and right is a point at 1 atm and 100 degrees C. Further up on the same branch is a point labeled critical point. This is at 218 atm and 374 degrees C. The area to the left of the left branch is labeled solid. The area between two branches is labeled liquid. The area to the right of the right branch is labeled vapour. The curve to the lower left of the triple point is labeled sublimation, the branch to the upper left of the triple point is labeled melting, and the branch to the upper right of the triple point is labeled boiling.

evaluation.notes: The phase diagram geometry, curve shapes, axis scaling, and all key annotations are faithfully reproduced with correct physics, and the slider/demo-step interactions are pedagogically strong; however, the default view is dominated by a blue liquid-region fill and a heating-path line that make it look substantially different from the clean source figure, and duplicate Melting/Boiling labels reduce label clarity.
action_items: Reduce the default region-fill opacity or start with all fills at zero so the step-0 state reads as a drop-in replacement for the static source image

Increase the offset of the 'Triple point' label further below-right of the dot to avoid collision with the sublimation curve and dashed guide lines

demo_steps.narration: Hold temperature just below 0 °C and raise the pressure slider. The point crosses the leftward-leaning melting curve and the highlighted region flips from solid to liquid — because that boundary has a negative slope, squeezing ice turns it to water.

demo_steps.title: Normal heating at 1 atm
demo_steps.narration: At 1 atm the horizontal path crosses the melting line near 0 °C (solid to liquid) and the boiling line at 100 °C (liquid to vapor) — the everyday sequence of melting then boiling.

demo_steps.title: Low-pressure heating: sublimation
demo_steps.narration: Drop the path below the triple-point pressure (0.006 atm). The horizontal line now crosses only the sublimation curve, so solid turns directly to vapor with no liquid stage.

demo_steps.title: Supercritical heating
demo_steps.narration: Raise the path above 218 atm, past the critical point. The line crosses no coexistence curve at all: liquid and vapor merge into one supercritical fluid, so there is no sharp boiling transition.

plan.keyInsight: Phase is not a property of temperature or pressure alone but of the (T, p) point's position relative to the coexistence curves — which is why a negatively sloped melting line lets pressure melt ice, and why the same heating produces boiling, sublimation, or nothing depending on the pressure of the path.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Render as an SVG diagram with nonlinear (visually log-like) axes: y ticks 0.006, 1, 218 spaced so 1 sits low and 218 near the top; x ticks 0, 0.01, 100, 374 with 0.01 hugging 0 and 100/374 spread right. Draw the three coexistence curves in a single red stroke meeting at a black filled 'Triple point' dot (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm) and the boiling branch terminating at a black filled 'Critical point' dot (374 °C, 218 atm); the melting branch must visibly lean LEFT of vertical. Add gray dashed guide lines from both dots to the axes and a dashed pair at (100 °C, 1 atm). Place italic serif 's', 'l', 'v' in the left, central-wedge, and right regions. Tag the curves with small curved arrows labeled Melting, Boiling, Sublimation. Overlay a draggable-looking state dot driven by the two sliders, tint the containing region with a soft translucent fill (e.g. blue-ish for l, gray for s, orange for v), and draw the constant-pressure heating path as a horizontal line with small markers + labels at each curve crossing. Keep axis labels and the H2O title in the original bold styling.

discrepancies: The melting curve is drawn as a straight line (linear formula 0.01 - 0.0075*(p-0.006)) whereas the source shows a smoothly curved line that bends more to the left at higher pressures
The sublimation curve extends below the x-axis and to the left of the plot area, whereas in the source it starts cleanly at the bottom-left corner of the plot
The boiling curve appears slightly more angular/segmented compared to the smooth curve in the source, due to piecewise linear interpolation between data points
evaluation.notes: The phase diagram is structurally faithful with all key elements (triple point, critical point, three coexistence curves, region labels, dashed guides, curved annotations) correctly placed, and the interactions are excellent (sliders, heating path with three modes, 5-step demo); the main geometric weakness is the linear melting curve versus the source's curved one.
action_items: Replace the linear melting curve formula with a curved function (e.g., quadratic or exponential in pressure) so the melting line visibly bends leftward at higher pressures, matching the source's characteristic water anomaly shape
Clip the sublimation curve to start at the plot boundary (bottom-left corner) rather than extending below the x-axis, matching the source composition
Consider using a smooth spline or more densely sampled Antoine-equation data for the boiling curve to eliminate the slight angularity visible in the rendered output
